chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, from Minhal al-Qassab, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Do not go out to meet (the traveler), for the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) forbade al-tallaqqi.' I asked: 'And what is the limit of al-tallaqqi?' He said: 'That which is less than a gadwah or a rawhah.' I asked: 'Then how much is the gadwah and the rawhah?' He said: 'Four farsakhs.' Ibn Abi Umayr said: 'And that which is above that is not tallaqqi.'

key_terms.أَبُو عَبْدِ اللَّهِ: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him).
key_terms.التَّلَقِّي: Meeting a traveler on the road to greet them or purchase their goods before they enter the city.
key_terms.رَوْحَةٌ: A measure of distance, roughly equivalent to a gadwah.
key_terms.غَدْوَةٌ: A measure of distance, roughly equivalent to a rawhah.
key_terms.فَرَاسِخَ: Plural of farsakh, a unit of distance used in classical Islamic texts.

ai.seo_question: What is the distance limit for the prohibition of meeting travelers (tallaqqi) in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the Prophet’s prohibition of *al-tallaqqi*—where merchants or travelers meet incoming caravans to secure goods or greetings—by setting a precise geographical boundary of four farsakhs (roughly 16–20 km) from the city limits. This definition reflects the practical realities of 8th-century trade routes, ensuring the ruling remains applicable to the specific economic conditions of the time while preventing exploitation of arriving travelers. The distinction highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on contextualizing legal boundaries based on measurable, observable criteria rather than abstract principles.
